utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, The Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Friday, July 18, 2008. First of all, good morning to the witness. Good morning also to the accused, the Defence counsel, and Mr. Stringer, as well as all the other representatives of the OTP, as well as everyone assisting us in this case. Today, we are going to complete the cross-examination of the witness. According to the numbers I have here, you have 38 minutes left, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel. Good morning, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When we finished yesterday, we were talking about a report which you wrote in August of 1993, in which you made reference to Muslims having been removed from their addresses or were not otherwise available for service of summons. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you another exhibit. This is P02802, which I believe is in the third binder. 2802, binder number 3. It appears, Mr. Buntic, that you can see it on the screen, and so while the usher is assisting us in locating the document -- okay, we've got it now. This is not one of your reports, Mr. Buntic. This is an activity report by a member of the military police, the commander of the 1st Company of the 3rd Battalion. This is a daily report for the 15th of June, 1993. I want to direct your attention, sir, to the last paragraph of the document, in which this gentleman, Mr. Mate Anicic states: "No criminal acts or incidents were notified yesterday, only the ethnically cleansing of the town of persons of Muslim nationality was noticed." Then he goes on to indicate that the perpetrators of this were members of the 4th Battalion and members of the ATG Baja Kraljevic. My question for you, sir, is: Isn't it true that there was a regular activity involving ethnic cleansing of Muslims from the west side of Mostar during this period, June and afterwards, throughout the summer and fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular ethnic cleansing, well, this is the first time I'm hearing of such a term, so I can't answer affirmatively. That's one. Second, I'm seeing this report for the first time, and I have to add that never, in the course of my work in the Justice and General Administration Department have I ever received a report from the Intelligence Service, SIS, the military police, the civilian police, or any other agency regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, sir, if this sort of activity was occurring in West Mostar, are we to understand that you, as the head of the Justice Department, did not know about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. I have never received from the civilian MUP, or the military police, or the Intelligence Service either a verbal or a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, my question now is a different one. Did you, in your capacity as head of the Department of Justice, did you know about this practice, did you know about these activities, did you learn about it from a different source?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have known as much as was reported in newspapers or inasmuch as it was discussed at government sessions, that is, HVO sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you work in West Mostar during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 16th of June. I'm not sure that HVO sessions were held at that time in Mostar. I believe they were held, a part of them, in Siroki Brijeg, but certainly not the address where the headquarters used to be, that is, the building of the Arrow [phoen] Hotel, where the HVO was based at this time. I think that was the case, but I can't be sure. This is the 16th of June. I believe we worked in different buildings that were more distant from the frontline, or perhaps it was Bijeli Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we looked at a document written by Mr. Maric, who was with the Mostar Military District Court. He indicated that during this first half, I believe, of 1993, the priority was to institute proceedings in respect of Muslim aggression. We've also looked at your reports on the operations of the courts during this period of time. Is it true, sir, that the ethnically cleansing of Muslims from West Mostar during this period was not a priority of the courts established by you under the auspices of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. It assumes that there was ethnic cleansing. He can put it in another fashion. We have a report over here, what the gentleman said. That's his version of the events. He hasn't testified. Now, if he wants to put it differently, that's fine, but the way it's stated, as if it's a fact, and I object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's a fair question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It isn't a fair question. It was a battle zone. That's the problem, and unfortunately Mr. Stringer hasn't been here throughout the trial to hear all of the evidence and what was happening in Mostar. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's an outrageously naive comment to make, if I could say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that the conduct referred to in this report you're looking at, the ethnical cleansing of the town from persons of Muslim nationality, was not a priority of the courts established under your Department of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have before you a document, don't you, a document from the president of a court? We discussed that issue yesterday. I believe I've answered this question. The president of the court determines the priorities of the court, and he compiled and submitted his report about that. What I was able to do in this connection was to inform a section of the Supreme Court and demand an inspection of the work of these courts. I'm telling you what was in my powers. Other possibilities for me to intervene in the work of the courts did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The next exhibit, unless there is a question about that one from the Bench, the next exhibit is P03571. This is not in a binder, I don't think. It's one of the loose ones that we were just distributing today. Mr. Buntic, you were shown this document during your cross-examination by counsel for Mr. Coric, and this is a report or a document, I should say, dated the 19th of July, 1993. It's over the signature of Mr. Valentin Coric, and what this document is doing is relieving four members of the military police of duty, relieving them of duty on founded suspicion that they had committed rape, finding that this conduct was detrimental to the military police, sentencing them to military detention of 30 days. Do you recall seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we have in one of the binders that we have reviewed over the past few days, something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were talking about various cases and prosecutions that were occurring in the courts, as reflected in the court registers that you were looking at. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit is P03536, which is in your binder. I think it's in the same binder, 3536. And while that's being found for you, Mr. Buntic, the question is this: The gentlemen who are referred to in this previous exhibit, 3571, Mr. Knezevic, Pazin Coric, Mario Coric, and Mario Busic, were you aware, sir, at the time they committed this rape, or alleged crime, they were the security team for Mr. Prlic, who was the president of the HVO at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you see that in P03536?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to follow from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the insinuation is that the 30-day sentence was as a result of Dr. Prlic or that Dr. Prlic condoned this conduct, I suggest we see other documentation to that, because the insinuation, I take it, at some point, was that Dr. Prlic was responsible for the 30 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. It seems to me you're getting up to plead in the middle of the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You don't have to. It's not for anyone to interrupt to point out, to make suppositions to -- okay what's the relevancy, what's the relevancy of this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the relevancy to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, we'll see, wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm asking what the relevancy. I'm objecting on the grounds of relevancy. I don't have to wait. He's got to respond. Why is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll respond, Mr. President, if you think it's necessary for me to say why we think this is relevant. I think it's quite evident why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's hear why it's relevant? If the insinuation is that Dr. Prlic was responsible for the 30-day sentence, let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the relevance, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As the witness has indicated, he looked at the previous exhibit on his direct examination. It was shown to him by counsel for Mr. Coric evidently to show that the Croats and members of the HVO were being prosecuted for committing crimes. It seems to us to be manifestly relevant if in fact members of the military police, committing rape, are, in fact, at the same time members of the security team for the president of the HVO, so that's the relevance of it. I think it shows a pattern or a culture within the HVO that is of high relevance in the Court's deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I'm looking at. I don't have to be a rocket scientist to figure out why it was being shown by counsel for Mr. Coric. First of all it's not that they were being prosecuted, but Mr. Coric is clearing showing outrage at the low sentence, clearly in his state of mind as someone who takes law enforcement seriously. That's number one. Number 2, you will see Dr. Prlic is not being addressed or not being copied with any of this. And, 3, it's a far stretch to insinuate that because these people are assigned to Dr. Prlic, that somehow he's related either to the rapes, which is what insinuation is or a to low sentence. It's pure sleaziness, in my opinion, and doesn't belong in this courtroom. Now, if he can tie it up without speculation, fine, but where's the proof? And that's why I objected to relevance. And it's not speech-making, Your Honour. It is a proper objection. What is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, a proper objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that a misunderstanding occurred in reading this document P03571. I don't know whether it's necessary for me to read it because the Judges can read it for themselves. The sentence of 30 days, as we can see from the document, relates solely to the disciplinary proceedings, and that is the maximum sentence -- maximum punishment for a disciplinary infraction. In the last sentence before the concluding paragraph, we read that the whole case was transferred to the military prosecutor, so we don't know what sentence was meted out to them ultimately in the criminal proceedings, but it is obvious that a separate trial was held for rape. The whole document was not read out until the end, and a misunderstanding occurred. The relevant piece is the case was given over to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Absolutely right, absolutely right. I suggest that Mr. Karnavas look at the paper properly before shouting into the courtroom. You spoke about the sentence and an outrage of Mr. Coric. I don't know where you get that from. Here, what we read -- please let me finish. What we read is that Mr. Coric sent it on to the public prosecutor, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's an outrage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, do you know how things like these are handled? There is a military disciplinary procedure and there's a criminal procedure, and that's what happened here and it's perfectly all right. This document does not give any ground for any irritation or on anybody else's part. You anticipate, and I don't think that's helpful to the work of the Court, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, in Blaskic, this matter was held nicely as far as the maximum being 30 days. That's number one. Number two, the insinuation is that these people because they are assigned to Dr. Prlic, Dr. Prlic has condoned this, that's the insinuation, and that's what I object to on the ground of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President, Mr. Karnavas has made his closing argument with respect to the document. I'm sure he'll make it again next year, but I think on the basis of the direct -- or the cross-examination of this witness by counsel for Mr. Coric, it's appropriate for the Trial Chamber to have the whole story or the rest of the story, more facts about this particular group of individuals, and that was the point of this -- of showing the witness P03536, which I should add is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buntic, in the time that's left, I want to talk to you a bit about some of the detention facilities that you've made reference to; prisons, detention facilities, whatever you want to call it. And I think we're going to have to go back into binder number 1 for P00292. P00292. It may be that we can just deal with this one on the screen, Mr. Buntic. This is one of the earlier documents, 3 July 1992, recognising, of course, that this is just after the successful operation in Mostar and Western Herzegovina, which resulted in pushing the JNA out of parts of this region. It's a decree on the treatment of persons who were captured in armed fighting. It indicates that the head -- I'm looking at Article 2, the head of the Justice and Administration Department, in cooperation with the head of the Defence Department and head of the Interior, shall designate the locations where prisoners shall be kept in accordance with the aforementioned Convention, which is a reference to the Geneva Convention on prisoners of war. And in Article three, the Defence Department shall be in charge of the facilities referred to in this decree. So, again, recognising this goes back to the earlier period before the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, it appears to me, sir, would you agree, that Justice, Defence and Interior also all played a role together in identifying locations where prisoners of war would be held, and then the Defence Department had the further responsibility of being in charge of those facilities once they were identified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is that -- is that essentially how the breakdown or the division of responsibility remained throughout the following months, 1992-1993, after the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims broke out; that is, Interior playing a role in identification or finding locations where prisons could be, but that Defence Department retains responsibility for administering those facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree has not been changed or supplemented. It remained in this form until the end of the existence of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next exhibit is P00452, which I think is in binder number 2. Mr. Buntic, this is a decision dated the 3rd of September, 1992, so it's about three months after the decree we just saw. It is a decision of the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and what's happening here is the establishment of the Central Military Prison for the HZ-HB to be located at the Heliodrom barracks outside of Mostar, appointing Mr. Pusic, Mile Pusic, as the warden. And then in the statement of reasons, indicating that this facility was found or -- to be used at the proposal of the head of the Legal and Administrative Department, which I take is you. So -- and I know you testified about this in your direct examination, about the procedures and preparation that went into setting up the Heliodrom to be a place where prisoners of war could be held. So would you agree with me, sir, that as indicated here, the Heliodrom facility was identified as a location to hold prisoners of war, based at least in part on the input received from you at the Department of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with that. If you read carefully this statement of reasons, the proposal of the Justice and General Administration Department was to separate civilian prisoners who were serving their sentences pursuant to legal and final decisions of the competent court from the prisoners of war who were held at that time in the civilian prison in Mostar at Ricina Street. So as it follows from this statement of reasons, the proposal of the Justice Department was to separate these two groups. It was not the proposal of the Justice and General Administration Department to set up a central military prison at Heliodrom. That location was not chosen or proposed by the Justice Department. The Justice Department did not propose the location at all for the military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll accept that, that distinction that you're making. If I could move you, unless there's a question about this document, to the next exhibit, P02972. I'm going to move ahead now to the period after the conflict began between the Croats and the Muslims. Binder 3. So we're moving ahead. And while the document is being found, Mr. Buntic, just a few questions. Do I understand correctly that the position of the Department of Justice was that military prisoners, that is, prisoners of war, should be held separately or detained separately from people who were in detention, having been convicted of crimes in the civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, so persons who were in prison or who were supposed to be in prison, pursuant to decisions of the regular courts, were put in the district prison in Mostar on Ricina Street. It existed before, and we had no other institution where prison sentences could be served, prison sentences imposed by civilian courts. This prison, as I've already indicated, was under the direct jurisdiction of the president of the Higher Court, and it was the only institution that was within the jurisdiction or under the jurisdiction of civilian courts, and it was supervised by civilian courts. There was no other institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have in front of you Exhibit P02972. This is a subject of a request dated the 26th of June, 1993, and it's a request directed to the Central Prison in Mostar, for Mr. Mile Puljic, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 2nd Brigade, and he's urgently requesting 20 prisoners, to have them perform works in the 1st Sector at the demarcation line on the Ricina Street, indicating that the 2nd Battalion would provide transportation and security. First question is, sir: Were you aware -- did you have any knowledge of the use of prisoners from the Central Prison, Mostar, to perform labour in the confrontation zone during the course of the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received two or three submissions in the Justice Department to the effect that the detainees or prisoners were taken out of the prison, and we responded promptly. A letter was signed to the governors and other institutions where we protested, and we insisted -- it was insisted that any such practice should stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So I take it, then, that indicates that you would condemn or would not approve of the use of prisoners to perform labour in this way.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those letters that we sent, this practice was condemned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, one last question, because at least my English translation is a bit vague. This is a request directed to the Central Prison, Mostar. Looking at this, can you tell you specifically are we talking about a civilian prison that was under the jurisdiction of the Justice Department, or are we talking about the military investigative prison facility at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that we received pertained to the persons who were at Heliodrom. The protest that we received and that prompted the Justice and General Administration Department to issue those letters protesting against this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And again just so that we're clear, are we talking about people who were in custody of the HVO military police; military prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate about that, about who put them there, how they were housed there at that location, because I've already indicated I don't have any reliable information about that; and I never received any documents from any official bodies that might have reported this to me. I categorically claim that the MUP, the military police and the SIS never informed me about that. If you find any such document, I'm perfectly ready to remain here in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P02679, 2679. And while that's being located, Mr. Buntic, this is a document dated the 8th of June, 1993, over the signature of Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and it's a decision to set up the county military prison and the county prison for the areas of Capljina, Neum, Ljubuski and Ravno municipalities, and setting up this at Gabela, and then indicating at the third paragraph that the decision comes into effect immediately. I believe, sir, that you saw this or looked at this in your direct examination. You indicated, correct me if I'm wrong, that you had never seen this before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if Dr. Prlic had, in fact, issued this decision to set up this prison facility in Gabela, you were not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, and I added that I don't recall that this decision was ever made at the sessions of the HVO. But if you remind me by putting to me the minutes from the session where it was actually made, I might be able to remember, but I really can't remember any such decision being made at any of the sessions of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke earlier about Gabela and also Dretelj, which I'll ask you about, and I want to make sure I understand correctly. Is it your testimony, sir, that the prison in Gabela was a misdemeanor prison that was under the jurisdiction of the municipal authorities exclusively?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you've seen, there are decisions made by the Capljina municipality to set up this prison where misdemeanor sentences were to be served, and as you could see, the persons remanded in custody were also to be put there, and this was a military facility. It was as early as in March 1993, and I am aware of this decision made by the Capljina municipality. I saw it before. It was published in the Official Gazette in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and as such, I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Prisoners -- let me ask you this. Is it possible that there are more than one prison facility that we're talking about in Gabela, one that was the misdemeanor prison run by the municipality authorities, and a different facility that was run by the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This scenario is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you look at the next exhibit, please, P10190. 10190, which is in the fourth binder. This is a certificate. It's signed by a gentleman named Ante Prlic, who I don't think you know, Mr. Buntic. It's dated the 22nd of August, 1993. And in this certificate, Mr. Prlic, who is a member of the military police, is submitting the certificate, requesting the release from detention of all Muslims who are in possession of letters of guarantee. He's actually referring to an order issued by the head of the military police, Valentin Coric, that these prisoners, whose names appear on the document, who are in Gabela Military Prison have to be delivered to the Ljubuski military police pursuant to the fact that their families are in Ljubuski and they got expulsion from Herzegovina. Were you aware, sir, of any practice whereby prisoners were being released from the Gabela Military Prison on the condition that they possessed letters of guarantee, that they would move to third countries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, and this document is -- this is the first time that I see this document, just as I have never seen the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you aware of a decision issued by Mr. Prlic on the 22nd of December, 1993, to close the Gabela Prison facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, and this decision was published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community or, rather, the Republic, as it was styled now, of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. If I could have a moment, Your Honour, I'm trying to consolidate here in order to meet the time limitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, could you please now turn to P03201. 3201, which is probably in binder 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Your Honour, I didn't want to intervene earlier. Perhaps I should have a couple of minutes earlier. The witness was talking about the detailed -- the witness was not asked about the specific situations in the Capljina municipality prisons in the direct examination, but he was only asked about the work of one commission -- or, rather, not the work of one commission, but they're going to the municipality. And at that time the witness said the only thing he knew about the fact that prisoners were kept or isolated persons were held in the municipality of Capljina was the information that he received from the president of the municipality in Capljina, as far as I can remember. Today, he told us a couple of minutes ago that he might be able to say something, but that he may be guessing that there may have been something in Gabela apart from the detention facility, something that would be under the control of the military wing. That's the way the question was phrased. I would like to know, in light of the documents that the Prosecution is trying to put forward, and there is another document coming and we insist that this is forgery, I would like the Prosecution to establish some kind of foundation to see whether he would be asking the witness about what he knows or what he might only speculate or guess about, because on the basis of what he told us about what he knew about the events in Capljina, he told us that he -- the only things that he knew about the situation in Capljina were the situations that he was told about by the head of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that the Petkovic Defence joins in with the Coric Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The objections are now in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This next do you, 3201, Mr. Buntic, you have it in front of you. It's dated the 5th of July, 1993, and it's written by someone named Obradovic, and he's directing this to the warden of a number of prisons, Gabela, Dretelj, Heliodrom and Ljubuski. And my question, sir, is whether you know that, in fact, in each of those locations there was a central military investigative prison that fell within the jurisdiction of the military police of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've already answered this question, and let me clarify what I said a moment ago. I said that this possibilities could not be ruled out. I did not insinuate anything else. I said -- that's what I said, quote/unquote, so I really don't know -- I didn't know how it was. I told you all I knew about Dretelj and Gabela, on the basis of everything that was published in the Official Gazette in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the decision that was made, that was published there. It's had its name, its full name, and I said quite specifically what it contained. And then I commented that I could not rule out that other things were happening, but that I cannot know anything about that. This order, this document, as well as the previous two documents, I have not seen them before, truly; so it is really difficult for me to comment on it. I think that you should bear this in mind. It's been 17 years, and now I first -- I see documents for the first time and I'm asked to comment on them. I don't think it's really fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not intervene before the witness gave his answer, and I did not want to affect his answer in any way, but I would just like to intervene as regards the Prosecution question, because the Prosecution is imputing that those prisons were under the auspices of the Defence Department, and I would like to note that this witness was asked directly under whose jurisdiction military prisons were, and he did not say that they were under the military police that was part of the Defence Department, so I think that this is a construct that is trying to impute things to the witness so that he could give his answer in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I can move on from this particular part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. Just for the record, of course, page 19, line 15, the last intervention was made by Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have five minutes left. Please move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If I could just have one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could direct you, sir, to Exhibit P03560, 3560. This is minutes of the 46th session of the HVO, held on the 19th of July, 1993, in Mostar. You were present, as well as other members of the HVO HZ-HB. Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is July 19th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm looking at item 7, which states here that after a discussion of the request by the HVO of the Capljina municipality to relocate prisoners, and a discussion of the status and accommodation of conditions of prisoners and prisons, persons in isolation, with the aim of improving accomodation, et cetera, unanimous approval was given to the following conclusions. And this conclusion was to secure accommodation conditions that were in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. If the existing accommodation conditions are not satisfactory, the head of the Justice and General Administration, in coordination with the Defence Department, shall designate new sites. And then continuing on, this is the working group. Now, you talked about this working group, and as I understand it, sir, what you did in response to this was to go down and talk to the municipality officials in Capljina and get information from them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It seems to me, sir, that you were not in a position to determine whether the existing accommodation conditions were satisfactory if, in fact, you never went to the camp itself. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did this on the demand of the Capljina municipality, and the conclusions of the HVO, I said that we visited the Capljina municipality, the president who was there with all his office heads. They told us the figures about the number of people who were there, the surface area of the premises, and all the problems that they had encountered. I said that I had refused to go there, and I gave my reasons, because I didn't think that I had any jurisdiction; and I did not have powers to go there. Those institutions, those facilities, were not under the control of the civilian judiciary, the civilian courts, which is why I did not have any powers to enter them at all. We received information, and on the basis of this information we drafted proposals for the HVO. The proposal was that on the basis of the information we obtained in the Capljina municipality, to release half of the people immediately and to relocate the other half to facilities which would provide better conditions. And this is why another group was set up, as you can see on the next page, to check out the situation in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would your answer be the same if I asked you if you ever went to other prisons, such as the Heliodrom facility, where prisoners of war or Muslim prisoners were being held, there was a central investigative military prison in Ljubuski? Do you about any of those?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated before this Tribunal that I visited Heliodrom only once, that it happened some time in June, late May or the first half of June, that I -- that the civilian prison was moved from Ricina Ulica to Heliodrom, and I gave the reason for that, that's because the prison in Ricina was at the frontline, that those people should be relocated from there. There was no other possibility but to set up a division of the civilian prison, which is where we moved some 20-odd civilian prisoners who were put in a special section at Heliodrom. I went there, I visited those people. There were only two people there who were not in the civilian division, two people who did not have final decisions, so that they could be there pursuant to final decisions. And I asked immediately, from the warden, to release them. So that was the only time I went to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My last question, then, is this: Are you aware, sir, that large numbers of Muslim civilians were arrested and placed in detention at the Heliodrom facility during the 9th, 10th and 11th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew this information, but I said that I had not received this information from any official institutions. I heard about it, that -- rumours from the press, from what people were talking about in the street, from conversations with my friends, my colleagues, general public. But I repeat once again, apart from what was discussed at government sessions, I did not receive any official confirmation of that, and there is no document from those institutions. And as I've already told you, if you manage to find a single document from those institutions, you can just put me in prison right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that if that happened, it was not within the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If a large number of Muslim civilians were rounded up and placed in detention in the Heliodrom on the 9th, 10th and 11th of May, 1993, such an operation or an activity would not have fallen within the competence of the Department of Justice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have been, had they been brought to the civilian prison in Ricina Street in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do have some redirect, Your Honours, and it would take me approximately five minutes to set up. We are rather organised. If we could take an early break at this point. I don't anticipate it being very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have the break now. That's no problem. For once, we have some time available. We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have the redirect now. The Chamber recalls, for the record, the time spent on redirect is deducted from the general time allocated to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and for the record we are fully aware of that, and we appreciate the reminder anyway. What we have prepared for you is a special binder. We actually have put it in order. You also have a sheet that tracks along the various chapters. I must caution Your Honours not to expect this on each and every occasion, because it -- we just happened to have some time to put this together. But, in any event, we hope to make it more efficient. We'll go through the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, again good morning. I just have a few question and I want to ask you to clarify some points in the testimony, and the first one I want to go to, it's in reference to a question that was asked by Judge Trechsel, if you may recall, and this was back on 10 July 2008. For the record, the portion of the testimony goes from pages 30575 all the way to 30586, though what is really pertinent is the question from Judge Trechsel on 30585, and this has to do with, Mr. Buntic, where you were discussing the fact that you had been assigned to look -- to Citluk to see whether the municipality -- bless, you Judge Trechsel -- to see whether the municipality could provide some alternative facilities for those who were detained. So do you recall that exchange, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And a question was posed to you, and I'm not sure whether you heard it right or whether you misunderstood the question. It was rather concrete. Judge Trechsel asked you whether the government had a possibility to expropriate property when it was needed for the purpose of the whole of the HVO. Now, you had indicated, prior to that, about property that belonged to the SFRY or the Yugoslav Army, so that the government or the HVO could take that at its disposal. But the question posed to you by Judge Trechsel, as I understood it, had to do with expropriating property within a municipality for the purposes of the HVO. And Judge Trechsel will correct me if I'm wrong on that. So I want to give you an opportunity now to answer that question. Was it possible for the government to expropriate property that belonged to the municipality? And if so, what would be the legal procedure in doing so, unless it was able to just simply snatch it and use it upon immediate request?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before, in practice the HVO did not make any decisions that would expropriate property belonging to SFRY or JNA. As for expropriation of property, in principle, that was done by municipalities, because they could -- in fact, the headquarters of the Territorial Defence could expropriate property. As for Citluk municipality, I know that for that purpose, Citluk municipality had already requisitioned the primary and secondary schools in Citluk to put up refugees from Central Bosnia and Eastern Bosnia. I know that from speaking to the president of the municipality about the accommodation of these persons in Citluk municipality. It is probably also known that Medjugorje resort was also expropriated for the purposes of the SFOR. So everything that the Citluk municipality was able to put at anyone's disposal was already taken up. In this resort, Kompas Medjugorje, UNPROFOR, later SFOR was accommodated, and the school building accommodated refugees from Eastern and Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now that we know a municipality could expropriate property belonging to the municipality or within its municipality, but my question, and I believe Judge Trechsel's question, had to do with the HVO HZ-HB being able to go into a municipality and expropriate. Was this some sort of a legal procedure that you would have to go through before the HVO HZ-HB, you know, the executive authority, could take hold of a property and use it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the regulations that we had, we did not have such possibilities, nor do I know that a case like that happened in practice, apart from the property that I said was the property of the Yugoslav People's Army and the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that answers the question or clarifies the matter. The next section I want to refer to parts of the transcript, I've -- I'll identify them for everyone and for the record we will be looking at pages -- where it starts the discussion on 30654 to 30662. This would be on the 14th of July, 2008, when you spoke. And this area -- this topic deals with the supervision and control of the various detention facilities and military prison facilities. You talked a little about it today, but I want to give you an opportunity to further develop that, consistent with your testimony that you gave us here today. And let me preface my question to make sure that I understand it. It is your testimony that when it came to facilities that housed prisoners of war, those were not under your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, and again if I understand you correctly, where someone had gone through an investigative process or was going through an investigative process, or was even in trial or sentenced, they -- those facilities were different, first of all, than facilities that housed prisoners of war, and, two, the presidents -- the respective presidents of the court that had jurisdiction were responsible for visiting those prisons and looking after the well-being to make sure that those detainees, prisoners, were being properly cared for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to leading questions on this redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking if he verifies that that is his testimony, so I'm not leading him into anything that he hasn't said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think, again, it's a leading question. We can clearly say that. And asking him to verify his evidence by putting propositions to him is simply leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, can you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will do it another way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the transcript, you are asked by counsel, Ms. Nozica, a question, and you said that: "Now, when it comes to the venues holding prisoners of war, that's where the Defence Department would have jurisdiction. Now, when it comes to -- when it comes to prisons, it's the president of the District Court and the warden of the prisons who have those facilities." And I'm quoting from page 30655, lines 6 through 10. Do you recall saying that, sir, and do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall saying that, and I stand by that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then at some point you were pressed, and on page 30657 you indicated that we could find the answers in Articles 30 to 35 of the Decree on the District Military Courts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the 17th October, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, because that chapter of the Decree on District Military Courts regulates the issue of serving sentences under decisions of district military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And now before we go into the actual documents, on page 30661, you were asked to look at Article 205 of the -- and this would have been 4D01105. That would be the Law on Criminal Procedure, Article 205, and a portion was read to you. And you don't have to look at it yet. We're going to go through this step by step. I just want to make sure that we have the foundation, since we received an objection that somehow I was leading you. It says here, on line 12, "It's a provision governing the issue of supervision over courts, over prisons -- sorry, and inmates." And then there's a quote where it says: "Supervision over prisoners in custody shall be exercised by the president of the court who's authorised to do so." And then you answer: "Yes, this confirms all the evidence I have given on the subject; namely, the presidents of the court, if we're talking about military courts, provide supervision, and when civilian persons are concerned, it's the president of civilian courts." And that's -- as I understand it, that is your position. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When we're talking about these military prisons, again to make sure that everybody's crystal clear, we're not referring to places that are housing prisoners of war, but rather these district military prisons; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In this case, we're talking about persons held in a military prison pursuant to decisions of the District Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, and then you pointed out -- you were pointed -- you were shown a document, and you can look at it very quickly if you wish, and that is 2D 1412, and this was a document that was generated by the warden of the District Military Prison, Slavko Aleksovski, and you pointed out quite clearly that this was merely his proposition and nothing more than that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's a proposal, as we can see from the reception stamp, that was sent to HVO Busovaca on the 30th of July, 1993, and it was indeed received. It's a proposal, therefore, from Central Bosnia, where the HVO was based in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go through some of the jurisprudence rather quickly. If we look at 4D 1105, that's in your binder, that's the Law on Criminal Proceedings. And you were referenced to Article 205. And for Your Honours, that would be on page 60 in the English version. If you could find that. And if you look at the bottom of the page, Mr. Buntic, it might be easier for you to find it under 4D 231089 are the last digits on the bottom of the page. So, Your Honours, if we could go back one page to page 59, just so we see the heading of this topic of articles, we see that it says: "Procedure with persons in pre-trial custody." I underscore "pre-trial custody." So now we know what 205, this section, is in, and we see -- and I'm going to read not just the first article, point 1, but also point 2: "Surveillance over prisoners in custody shall be exercised by the president of the court who's authorised to do so. 2. The president of the court or judge, whom he designates, must visit persons in custody at least once a week and should it be deemed necessary, inform himself when the warden and guards are not present, as to how the persons in custody are being fed, how their other needs are being met, and how they're being treated. The president or judge whom he designates must take the steps necessary to correct irregularities noted in the visit to the prison. The investigating judge may not be the judge designated. 3. The public prosecutor may also be present during the visit referred to in paragraph 2 of this Article. 4. The president of the court and the investigating judge may visit all persons in custody at any time, may talk to them, and may receive complaints from them." Now, let me go back, having read this. This was shown to you -- part of it was shown to you -- part of Article 205 was shown to you, hence why I asked the question initially before I drew the objection. Could you please tell us what exactly Article 205 is requiring the president of the court or the judge whom he designates to do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am required to give a brief answer, he is asked to supervise the prison in his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can we conclude, based on this reading of this, that when somebody is in custody during the pre-trial phase, that there is an obligation, at least by the judge, to visit the prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again it's a leading question. We all have the text, and it's not clear that the witness really can shed any more light on what it says or what his own interpretation of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We know what the practice is, Mr. Buntic, or what the practice was based on Article 205. For those who haven't practiced or are unacquainted with the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina or the former Yugoslavia as it existed, could you please explain? This is when somebody's under the decision of an investigative judge, being investigated. Could you please tell us, are there any obligations to look after the well-being of those being detained while they're being investigated, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I can say that before the war, in practice, things worked as they were prescribed to work by virtue of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final question. With respect to this, just to make sure I understand, if somebody is being detained as a prisoner of war in another detention facility, as you've indicated they would have to be, under Article 205 would a judge or prosecutor be under an obligation to monitor the well-being of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that obligation does not follow either from this law or from the decrees enacted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If they had no obligation, could you tell us whether they could have, nonetheless, if they wanted to; in other words, show up, show their credentials as being a member of the judiciary? Could they then have used that as a basis for having access to such a facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure they would have been able to gain access.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at the next document, and this is P00592, P00592. I'm going to show you a set of documents, and then at some point we'll have to double back, perhaps, to answer another question that was raised yesterday on these documents, but for a different reason. And I am told, Your Honours, that the translation should actually read more like: "The Decree on Executing Criminal and Misdemeanor Sanctions." At least that's what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at Article 30, this is in P00592. Look at Article 30, and it says here: "Sentences pronounced by the district military courts and in the case of appeals by the High Court or Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, shall be imposed in accordance with the provisions of the Decree on the Application of the Law on Sentencing and Fines under an Imminent Threat of War or in Times of War, and we see it's in reference to the Official Gazette of the Republic of BH 6/92. Have you had a chance to read Article 30, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and it's correctly quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us what exactly Article 30 is telling us here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, it says that sentences and fines are in imposed in keeping with the legislation and regulations of the Bosnia-Herzegovina that have been in place, and certain exceptions are cited with regard to military courts that had just been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you look at 1D 02909, 1D 02909 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I would just like to be sure what the term "imposed" here means. I have the feeling that it means meted out sentences measured pronounced. It does not refer to execution. And I would like, Mr. Buntic, for you to tell me, is that the correct understanding, that this speaks of how the court commute -- figure out what sentence they will pronounce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it says "meted out," the term in Croatian is "izrecene." The term "final court decision" or "judgement" could not be used because there was a possibility that according to a decision of an investigating judge, a person is remanded in custody, so the remand in custody could have followed from a decision. So we could not say "enforcement of final judgements." Instead, there is reference to sanctions meted out, and "sanctions" is a broader term than "sentence," literally punishment, and that is the term that was used in the federal Law in the Enforcement of Criminal and Misdemeanour Sanctions and in the Republic law of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was later taken over by the regulatory documents of HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to be sure, Mr. Buntic, sentence imposed is what the judge reads out at the end of the trial, together with the judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Izreka" can also be translated as disposition of a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this line of questioning begs me to ask the question: When we look at this Article 30, are we to assume that we need to look at this Law on Sentencing and Fines Under Imminent Threat of War that's in the BH Official Gazette? That's what's being applied, is it not, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so we're going to cover this again, but so here is an example, for instance, where no changes, at least in Article 30, are made to republic law, but rather it is just being taken over, and under Article 30 that law must be applied?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and that follows from Article 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at that law, and we have 1D 02909 -- and by way of an explanation, Your Honours, you will see that this is from the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I must apologise for not having time to translate certain documents, but we did go on-line, and we did have what was actually adopted, as we can see from the Official Gazette on 15 June 1992. And we can put it on the ELMO, but perhaps I could ask one question. Sir, in looking at this Official Gazette copy of this law, is this what we're referring to in Article 30, The Law on Executing Criminal and Misdemeanor Sanctions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we compare this law and the issue of the Official Gazette where it was published, we will see that it's indeed the law taken over by this decree of HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And lest there be any misunderstandings, Your Honours, and again with the greatest of apologies, if we could just put on the ELMO two documents just to -- and the gentleman can read, and we can have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm a bit confused, Mr. Buntic, because we have just had an article which refers to the sentencing, to an act of the court, and now we have before us a law on the execution of sentence, which is a completely different method that in time comes once the sentence has been imposed. Also, I do not see that this law here refers to times of war and emergency. Well, I think both counsel want to explain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to explain this, because once again it's an issue of translation again. In Article 30 of the previous document, the name of the law was mis-translated. If the witness should read Article 30, para 1, you will see that it is the one -- the same law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was going to present these two documents, which may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. If I may intervene, I'm really a little bit confused and I would like to seek some clarification. Article 30 reads about the decree law on the application of the law on the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor sanctions during the an imminent threat of war; but in front of us we only have the Criminal Law on the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor sanctions that applied in peacetime. I allow for the possibility that it may be the same law, but I am a little bit confused, and that is why I support and endorse what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at the first -- what's on the ELMO, Mr. Buntic, because if we look at Article 30, you'll see what is being referenced, and you'll actually see the Official Gazette. And of course I wanted to make sure that -- you see the highlighted portion, 115. Could you read out that title? That might help us out here.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "115. Decree law on the application of the law on the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor sanctions during an imminent threat of war or state of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to the next document, if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I remain confused, because this is not what we have on document -- on the document 1D 02909, and I don't know how -- where the number 115 comes in, because I don't find any reference to that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is an Official -- this is a copy of the front page of the Official Gazette. Judge Trechsel, I don't mean to be disputatious today, I really don't. I know we got off on the wrong foot. But if I would be allowed to at least finish what I'm trying to do, and then if you're still confused, ask me questions. But right now, it gives the impression that somehow, you know, we're either terribly unorganised here or, you know -- you know, we just don't know what we're doing. And I do think that we have a certain system. We're trying to help you. You can see we've spent all night preparing, and I would beg you to let me finish this portion and then ask all the questions you want. But let me just finish, because I think it might become clearer. I had the same questions last night, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I only try to understand step by step, and now I'm jumping at your invitation, and I'm hoping we'll land softly. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the next document, Mr. Buntic, okay, because we're trying to figure out all of this, and maybe you could help us out. What does this read? What law are we looking at? And we could probably start with the date above.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows from this that -- well, let me read the full title: "Decree law on the application of the law on enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor sanctions in an imminent threat of war or state of war." We can see the heading, the header. It's: "Monday, the 15th of June, 1992, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just look -- now let's go back. Let's go to 1D 02909. And we might have it wrong, but I'm trying to figure this out. If we look at 1D 02909, we see this law is on executing criminal and misdemeanor sanctions. Now, my question is: When we're talking about Article 30, are we -- is Article 30 referring to this law from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was taken over by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, it is one and the same law. And as we have seen, it was adopted by a decree on the adoption of this law that we saw as the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to get to the technique that's used in BiH in a moment. Now, if we look at just Article 1, that's all I want to point to the Judges' attention at this point and we'll move on, it says: "Article 1. Sanctions, security measures and other measures pronounced in a criminal proceedings as well as misdemeanor sanctions and security measures pronounced in misdemeanor proceedings. Further on (sanctions) shall be in accordance with this law if not regulated differently in a special law in the organisation and work of the correctional facilities and penitentiaries, further on penal correction organisations shall hereby be defined." From Article 1, can you please explain to us, in simple terms, what exactly is it saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult for me to add anything to this article. I think that it speaks for itself. It is quite clear, and it confirms everything that we have been saying, because the terminology used here is the terminology used in the decree on district military courts of the HZ-HB, and it is merely specified here what sanctions, forms of punishment, security measures and other measures. All this could be subsumed under one and the same term, and that is "sanctions," because it says "other measures imposed" or "pronounced," "izrecene," it's the same term that is used in the decree of the HZ-HB, and it goes on to say "in criminal proceedings and in misdemeanor proceedings," talking about misdemeanor sanctions, "and protective measures shall be enforced in accordance with the provisions of this law, if not regulated differently in a special law." And it goes on to say: "... and the organisation and work of correctional facilities and penitentiaries," correctional facilities were mostly used for minors, for juveniles, "shall hereby be defined." I don't know if that's what you wanted me to explain, but that's what I thought it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fine, and again this is for clarifying your testimony. And now I want to go to P03350, and this is a work report from 1 January 1993 to 31 June 1993. And I want you to look at point 13. It's on page 3 in the English version. And I want to give you an opportunity to explain to us a little bit, keeping in mind what we have just discussed. You indicate on point 13: "Our contacts --" Or it's indicated. I don't know if it's being indicated by -- yes: "Our contacts with the prison wardens and commanders are almost nonexistent, so that we do not have information about the condition of people being held there on the basis of decisions issued by judicial organs." Now, you're making this reference to what is being talked about above. You go on to say: "Accepting the complexity of the situation and not wishing to interfere in defence work, we request complete information on the number of persons being held in prison and that we supervise the work of the prison, at least in the part that relates to the above-mentioned persons." They know you go on to say: "There are a certain number of cases when wardens and commanders do not adhere to court rulings. There is no justification for such behaviour." Now, earlier you told us that a judge, for instance who had to supervise, based on 205, had an obligation with respect to military district prisons, if it was a military matter -- a military court or judge, or in civilian prisons, but here it would appear -- I mean, you indicated to us that that same judge would not have an obligation and most likely could not have access to prisoners of war so could you please explain to us, in point 13, what exactly are you trying to say in your report, because I do believe it might give the Court in guidance.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that what is stated in item 13 is quite comprehensible and clear. The only thing that perhaps begs some clarification is this part where it says "at least as far as the persons named above are concerned." Those are persons that were in those prisons on the basis of decisions issued by judicial organs, as indicated in the previous item, so the Justice Department sought information or sought to be granted access to the information about the status of the persons -- civilian persons put in Heliodrom detention facility, at least those who were there pursuant to final decisions of the judicial organs and who were there, as we've already heard, because the Ricina Street prison was at the frontline and had to be moved to the special civilian division of the District Military Prison at Heliodrom. So if any clarification was needed, it was for this one. As for the rest, I think it is quite clear, the meaning of item 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final point. Did the law provide for prisoners of war to be mixed up with regular prisoners or convicted individuals, or were they to be kept separated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to be housed in separate facilities, so prisoners of war were to be housed in separate facilities separate from the facilities -- prison facilities which housed persons who were there pursuant to the sanctions imposed on them in criminal proceedings, or if we're talking about misdemeanor proceedings, then there were special institutions in place for serving misdemeanor sanctions. So the law envisaged those options.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, by way of example, let's look at 1D 01797. 1D 01797. You may have looked at this before. And this is dated 8 November 1993. It's a report on inspection of detainees at the Ljubuski Military Remand Prison, and here we see, for instance, paragraph 1: "On 6 November 1993, the president of the Mostar District Military Court, pursuant to Article 205 of the ZKP Code of Criminal Procedure adopted by the Decree, performed an inspection of detainees at VIZ in Ljubuski. "On this occasion, it was established that the detainees are being adequately fed and supplied with other needs, and that treatment of the detainees is in accordance with the Code." And then the president goes on to say: "The president of the Mostar District Military Court spoke personally with the number of detainees, without the presence of overseers or guards." And then there's a reference to a person named Daka, aka Daka of Ljubuski, who was not in custody, although an in-camera decision had been passed that it extended the accused's detention, and apparently he was released without authorisation. Based on this document, making reference to Article 205, we have a district military court, we have the Mostar District Military -- the president of that court visiting, speaks of detainees at a military -- being kept at a military remand prison, is this making reference to POWs or is this making reference to prisoners that are in the process of being -- that are in the criminal proceedings, to put it in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abbreviation used here, "VIZ," this should be the military investigative prison or military remand prison, but -- so this is not an institute where people serve their sentences, but where they're remanded in custody before their trial. At least that would follow from this document, where the president of the District Military Court went to inspect and run some checks on the situation in the prison and then drafted a report on this visit, invoking Article 205 that gives him such powers. I don't know whether this is sufficient, but what I can see from this document would lead me to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So that we do not get too far away, Mr. Buntic, we had Article 205 of that code. Here we have a report of an inspection. This is an application of 205. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president invokes Article 205 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the ZKP, and we can see that he is drafting his report, and we can see who the report is sent to, the report containing his observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The previous document, we've seen your report with that paragraph 13. Does this concern the same? Is this also in connection with Article 205? You remember, you complain there on scarce contacts with prison wardens and commanders. Does that concern also the area covered by Article 205?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't say that this was under Article 205 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, because Article 205 of the Law on Criminal Procedure deals with the rights and obligations of the presidents of the courts in relation to their legal powers to enforce various sanctions, so we're talking about the powers of the court presidents, and the powers of the Justice Department would not follow -- would not stem from this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe there is an error somewhere. I would put it to you that Article 205 exactly does not deal with the execution of sanctions, but with deprivation of liberty within the frame of criminal procedure as detention on remand, detention of persons who are still presumed to be innocent. So there is categorical differences between one and the other. Would you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. I had a better look, and I can agree with you that -- I have already said that you can see, from the very name of this institution, that it is a remand facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just as an aside, since we're on these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just as an aside, since we're on these documents, yesterday, on page 41, you were asked a question; and I'll read it because it's short, and you gave an answer, and this had to do with the taking over of legislation, of laws, from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the question was: "Well, I think the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted the Yugoslavia code, because it was now a new state entity. I mean -- and let's put it -- let me put that to you. It seems to me that this decision or this decree implies that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna thinks it is a new form of entity, such that it is necessary to adopt or cede to another form of legislation that has previously applied in the territory?" Now, your answer was: "This warding was used in enactment of all regulations and cases when and intervention was needed in existing regulations. The regulation was first taken over in its entirety and then a modification was made to only that part which needed to be modified. So I don't see anything special with this decree, compared with other decrees, or the technique applied throughout the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. There's nothing peculiar about this decree that would not have been in any other decree. I've told you already that this was done the way it was, and I said why." Now, as a perfect example of what you were trying to convey to us yesterday, by serendipity, the law that we just looked at, if you look at Article 30; and we don't have to spend too much time, it made reference to a law that was passed by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that it had actually taken over from the Socialist Republic, as we saw, and in Article 30 we don't see that any changes were necessary -- were made; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the ones that -- where changes were made, the ones that you were pointing out, the ones that -- the changes that we actually did see dealt with the fines and the monetary value that had to be -- the currency and the value of the fines, but the rest of the laws remained intact as they were; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They could have stipulated that the feathers of the paradise bird would be the next legal tender, but we couldn't catch the paradise bird.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we move on to my next topic, this has to do with statutory decisions, and I'm going to reference you and reference everyone to parts of the transcript from 16 July 2008, pages 53 all the way to 57. I'm giving you the entire bundle, so you'll have context. And you were questioned about a document under a "P" number, P00303, and we have also translated it as 1D 00156. We prefer our translation, but it doesn't -- for our purposes, it doesn't make much of a difference. Now, you were pointed to Article 9 in this particular document, 303, and again it doesn't make a difference whether you look at P00303 or 1D 00156, but if we look at Article 9, you were asked a question about that article, and you said -- a question was being posed: "And in this document --" this is on line 15, Your Honour, page 55: "Okay. And in this document, there appears to be a change or a shift in the language indicating here that the president is accountable for the work of the HVO. There is no reference to collective aspect; would you agree with me?" And your answer was: "In Article 9, yes, that's correct. The contents of Article 9 are as you just presented them." Question: "Okay. And now as you've just indicated, it was at the following session of August 1992 that Mr. Prlic was then appointed to be the president of the HVO?" And you said it was correct. Then on page 56, you're asked again about Article 9. This is on line 7: "Okay. Would you agree with me, sir, that Article 9 here applies and governs the work of the HVO from this point on, 3rd of July, 1992, until the end of the Croatian Community in August 1993, when the Croatian Community became the Republic -- the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?" At that point, you say: "I have to apologise for something. This document that I have in front of me is a document dated 3rd of July, 1992." You then go on, on page 57, and this is what I -- we will discuss, where you say -- it goes: "Now, you realise that you were referring to another document?"
