You say: "I think that we have another document regulating the internal structure or organisation of the Croatian Defence Council, and I think that this document should be seen in the context of that document," meaning 303 should be seen in the context of the other document: "And that those two documents regulate the jurisdiction and the purview of the Croatian Defence Council and of its departments. So it's not only this document; there are two documents that have to be looked at, the interrelation between the two." Now, do you recall giving that corrected answer, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I said this is not the only regulation stipulating the powers of the HVO; that it needs to be viewed instead in correlation with the earlier decision of the 15th of May. And I said I thought from the start that's the document we were dealing with. And also in correlation with the amendments and decision of the 17th of October, 1992. So these would be the documents that form the framework for the powers, responsibility and structure of the HVO, because we have seen there are different periods and different documents, and in those different periods the rights and obligations and the structure of the HVO differed, and the internal organisation and the responsibilities and powers of the HVO had to be viewed in the context of all these documents. That's what I meant to say. I don't know exactly what was recorded, but that was my idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at 1D 00001. This is our first document for the Defence. This is a decree on the organisation and responsibilities of the departments and commissions of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And if we look at the last page, we'll see that it's dated 14 August 1992, signed by president of the HVO and HZ-HB, Mate Boban. When you were referring to another document that regulates -- sorry, I'll use your correct language -- regulating the internal structure or organisation of the Croatian Defence Council, were you referring to this document, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so if we want to interpret Article 9, for instance, in a proper context, then we would have to look at this particular decree; is that your position, based on the answer that you gave to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I believe we've covered that issue. We'll move on to the next topic. The next topic deals with transfer of power. That's what we've called it, actually. And first let me go to -- direct everybody's attention to the transcript of 17 July 2008, page 13, and here you are asked a question, and we need some clarification. Hopefully you might be able to assist the Trial Chamber. You were asked by the Prosecutor: "And prior to the 17th of October, 1992, the HVO did not have authority to enact decrees, decisions, conclusions, et cetera. Only the Presidency could do that; correct?" Answer: "Correct." "And then after the 17th of October in 1992 that authority to issue decrees, decisions, enactments, et cetera, was given to the HVO HZ-HB?" Answer: "Correct. It's this decision of the 17th October whereby these powers were transferred to the HVO, and if those were decisions, they needed to be taken urgently in situations that bore no delay." Question: "Okay. But as we know, in reality what happened was that the HVO enacted scores, perhaps hundreds of decrees, decisions, et cetera, in the time that followed the 17th of October until the establishment of the Croatian Republic?" Answer: "Correct, and all these regulations are described in that list that has already been exhibited in this case during my earlier testimony." And, of course, all of this, this exchange, had to deal with -- dealt with, for the record, the P00684. Now, I want to look at -- we'll go back to P00303, if we could, and -- or 1D 00156. It doesn't make a difference. If you could find that document, sir. And I would like to direct the Trial Chamber's attention, because it may have escaped their attention - few things do, but this may have - Article 18. Article 18, this is 3 July 1992. This is before any amendments. Article 18 reads as follows, and help me out if I mis-read it: "The HVO shall issue decrees, decisions and conclusions to regulate economic and other relations in the territory of the HZ-HB." Do you see that, Mr. Buntic? I know it's been a long time since you've actually had to read these documents, but it's there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from here, it would -- we could conclude that perhaps you erred when you indicated that it wasn't until the decision on amending the statutory decision, and that was -- as we discussed earlier, that was P00684, and of course we all have to understand that, one, your health is not the best and that you are tired as well from giving evidence; but would it be fair to say, sir, that even prior to the amendment, the HVO had the capacity to issue decrees, decisions and conclusions not only for matters to regulate economic relations, but other relations as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's evident from this article. It refers -- it states explicitly that the HVO shall issue decrees, decisions, conclusions, et cetera, and in keeping with this Article 18 of the 3rd of July, 1992, HVO did have such powers and was able to issue such regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, by way of a vignette or two as an example, if we could look at 1D 00015. This is dated September 1992, and here is a directive, and this has to do with -- we see at the end that we see your name, head of the department, "Zoran Buntic," and we see that this is a directive on making storage, using and keeping of record stamps. Correct? So here we have this is sort of -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next topic. This has to do with districts, the [indiscernible] or whatever you want to call it, because I believe you were in the process of giving an answer and you were interrupted. And so I want to make sure that you have an opportunity to fully complete what you were trying to convey to us when you were interrupted, and for that I'm going to refer to the transcript from 17 July 2008, page 34 to, actually, 36. Initially, you were being questioned concerning -- you were shown a document, P00250 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Counsel, I apologise for the interruption. Mr. President, I have noticed that one of the accused has left the courtroom. Perhaps the record should reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Praljak has left the courtroom for an urgent reason. He'll come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm in my own little world at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Could you open a window and let out the number of the document you are using?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Right now, I was looking at page 34 of the transcript, Your Honour, from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. We haven't got to the document, but we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked a question about in the various municipalities where you had, you indicated that HVO would be operating and at the same time, for the Muslims, there would either be a crisis staff, a war presidency, it came under various different names, and then at some point you were asked by the Prosecutor: "Well, that sounds like a very harmonious process." And you indicated, in a sense, that, well, it was until at some point, and you say, and this is on page 36: "After a while, that state of affairs, through a natural course of things, led to a conflict. The conflict between Croats and Bosniaks occurred, and the Muslims or the Bosniak side, using the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its securities services, tried forcibly with its army and police to implement the degree on districts. That's something that the Bosniak side accepted as its own arrangement. After the Vance-Owen Plan that was accepted by both sides, the Croats and Bosniaks accepted the provinces as defined in the Vance-Owen Plan which were not the same as districts. That is when the conflict occurred, when each side tried to impose their own arrangements --" And then you were interrupted. Do you recall that exchange, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I must apologise for not having a Croatian version of this agreement, but we have seen it before. It's 1D 02903. That's for everyone. But were you aware that an agreement had been signed concerning the Vance-Owen principles - there were nine constitutional principles -and this was dated March 3, 1993; and it was signed by Alija Izetbegovic, Mate Boban, Haris Silajdzic, and Mile Akmadzic. Were you aware of that agreement, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is that what you were referring to when you said they had accepted the provinces based on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And I believe we can move on to the next document, and that would be 1D 01182. 1D 01182. These are minutes from 27 February 1993, and if we look at, if you have it, if we look at -- and the English version is page 2, and it's item number 4. We see it says: "It was stated that illegitimate decisions have been adopted for a long time in the Republic of BH government because the prime minister and Croatian ministers have not participated in their adoptions. For these reasons, the HVO and the Croatian people do not recognise the decisions of the incomplete government of BH. One of the reasons for the HVO's position is the recent letter sent by Minister of Energy, Mining and Industry in the Republic of BH government, Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic and signed by Interior Minister, Jusuf Pusina, and chief of the BH OS Main Staff, Sefer Halilovic and addressed to the commander of the BH, 4th Corps, in Mostar. This letter contains obvious elements of a classic coup d'etat, because it uses a harmless (economic) heading to ask their military units to form new organs of civilian government and appoint management staff and enterprises." Now, is this what you were indicating yesterday when you indicate at some point they were trying to impose these districts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interrupted at the moment when I was about to utter a word that I see was not recorded; namely, that an attempt was made to do it in a forcible, armed fashion. I was interrupted, so these words did not enter the record yesterday. We see the document now. We have had other documents before us that were exhibited, from which it is evident that Minister Mahmutcehajic and Sefer Halilovic, a military commander, sent a letter to Arif Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps, and the security service, that is, the police, instructing them to implement forcible military measures to establish the district of Mostar; and all this is happening just after the highest representatives of both the Croat and the Bosniak peoples had signed an agreement that implies a different organisation according to the Vance-Owen Plan of provinces accepted by both sides, those provinces being very different from the districts that they tried to impose. Of course it had to lead to a conflict. We are all lawyers here in the courtroom, and we all know what a signed document by highest representatives of both communities should mean. Instead, we see that a pretty insignificant minister from that government and a military commander are sending orders to the army and the police to use military ways to establish a certain state organisation that runs counter to the highest enactments signed by the highest authorised representatives of both communities. Of course it had to lead to a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And, Your Honours, I'm going to skip the documents that actually go to this topic, which are 1D 02565, P01661, 1D 01972, 1D 0059 [sic]. They have been discussed before, and we will discuss them again in this context, but to just move on to the very last topic, and it deals with mobilisation. And this is sort of more of a vignette than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by Judge Antonetti on page 56 -- he said: "Yes, but you have not answered my question. When you have court, you need judges, and you appointed a number of judges. But for these judges to do their work, you need lawyers, defence counsel. How many of these were there?" And you indicated -- you said: "In light of what I said before, the scarcity of judges, we were forced to mobilise lawyers in order to be able to full vacancies" or "fill vacancies in courts and somehow create preconditions for the judiciary to operate at all, so we fill vacancies simply by mobilising lawyers. There was no other way." Do you recall giving that answer, Mr. Buntic? You recall giving that answer, do you not? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give such an answer. I am just not sure that it was properly recorded, because now in interpretation, I heard the word "lawyers," whereas I used the word "advocates." I was talking about attorneys, advocates. They were forced to mobilise one number of the attorneys or advocates needed. Perhaps there was a mis-interpretation either yesterday or today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, I'll ask you a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When we're talking about advocates, we're talking about folks who have actually taken the Bar, versus what is referred to in Bosnia-Herzegovina as graduated lawyers, someone who has gone through law school and may be practicing law, but not with a Bar license, and they don't usually have audience in court? I'm told there's a wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, to save some time, what's the difference between an advocate and a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lawyer in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, was considered to be a person with a law degree. For a person with a law degree to become a judge, a prosecutor, or a litigating attorney, in addition to a law degree, they had to have certain experience in legal jobs and to take the Bar exam. And after that, more practice was needed, one or two years, usually two years, in order to be able to open a law office and acquire the status of an advocate. So an advocate was a person who had these prior qualifications and was registered as a person practicing law and advocacy, that is, litigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going back to the question that was posed to you by Judge Antonetti. Let's look at 1D 02341 as an example of the conditions under which the judiciary operated in some places. 1D 02341. We see that this is the Stolac Lower Court. It's to the HZ HVO Department of Judiciary and General Administration, and I'll read portions of it, of this report. It says: "Judges who are appointed to the court in early 1993, after the court moved to Capljina because of the war. A large number of materials, land registers and active case files were salvaged from Stolac. None of the former employees remained with the court, and after some time the former president of the court also left the court, and the only two judges, with no other personnel, have been working over the past period. A large number of pending prewar cases were found in the court, and a record listing of the cases is currently being made." This I point out to the Judges of this honourable Tribunal: "The two judges are frequently engaged on the frontline in Stolac. Despite these conditions, in spite of the work of the two judges, the court has in this period carried out the following:" And we see what they have done. Mr. Buntic, to your knowledge, is this a fair and accurate representation of what was happening in the Stolac Lower Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Lower Court in Stolac, I am aware of what was going on there. We know what happened there first. First, the Yugoslav Army entered the Stolac area, expelled and made it impossible for anyone to work there, and then in June, late June 1992, conditions were once again in place for the institutions to start working again after Stolac was liberated. A year later, Croat-Bosniak conflicts break out in the same area, so the court was in a position to be able to operate normally for maybe seven or eight months; and in that period of maybe six or seven months we can see what work was done. They did over a hundred -- 132 on-site investigations. We can see that efforts were made to make it operational again, but as we said, a year after they started working again, or some ten months later, they had to relocate again and open the court in Capljina because of the Croat-Bosniak conflicts. The situation was similar in other areas that were affected by the war. We may have had just a couple of municipalities where municipal courts were able to work normally and without any disruptions, such as the court in Ljubuski, which is why we had only two judges working there, or why we set up the court in Tomislav Grad which throughout the existence of the HB HZ there was only one judge working there, because we had to deploy our personnel in other areas, civil courts, military courts, and to keep the whole judicial system functioning in some way. We made efforts, but we didn't have enough personnel. And as you can see, we had to mobilise some of the attorneys at law. But there were enough attorneys at law to defend their clients in civil lawsuits and criminal proceedings. That's what I didn't say yesterday. But I think that about half of the attorneys at law who had their own law offices were able to continue with their practice, but we had to mobilise the remaining half in order to keep the courts functioning at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I want to thank you very, very much. I have no further question, and I want to apologise for misrepresenting to you that you would be here for a few days. I should have said "a few weeks." But I believe that the Trial Chamber has benefitted immensely from your presence here, and I wish you the best in your future endeavours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break now. After the break, Mr. Praljak's Defence will intervene as part of the 92 ter procedure, and Mr. Kovacic, I believe you asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. My colleague, Nika Pinter, will examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session. Ms. Pinter, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In front of you, you have a document bearing the number 3D 03216. Is this the statement that you gave at the request of General Praljak's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you give this statement voluntarily, to the best of your knowledge and recollection, and is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to give us some additional clarification at page 2 of your statement. In the English version, I sign the relevant part of the statement that -- underlined the relevant parts of the statement, where you said that you tendered your irrevocable resignation. And I want to ask you why you did that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave some reasons why I tendered this resignation irrevocably in my testimony. That was because of the fact between the 9th and 19th of September, 1991, and the beginning of April 1992, the Citluk municipality was in a situation to defend itself alone. It stood against the Yugoslav Army that was massed on the northern borders of the Citluk municipality. The Brotnjo Battalion fighters were exhausted, fatigued. They had suffered casualties. They had wounded and killed. The neighbouring municipality of Ljubuski, which also had a 95 Croatian majority, as we saw from the documents, had an order in place that none of its citizens of military age should leave the municipality. I brought this to the attention of people in Citluk and in Ljubuski, and I also brought it to the attention of Mate Boban, who at that time spent more time in Citluk than in Grude, because the fighting was going on in Citluk, at its northern borders, and if this line were to be broken, the JNA would be able to link up with the barracks in Capljina. And as far as they were concerned, their war would be over in Herzegovina and parts of Western Herzegovina. Based on the map that all the reservists had on them, that we found later, indicating that the Mostar municipality and parts of the municipality of Capljina were drawn in, annexed to Montenegro. So we did have this information, we were aware of it, and despite all those warnings, demands and talks, nobody came to our aid. And in this situation, which was absurd and impermissible, I tendered my irrevocable resignation not only to the post of the commander of the defence of Citluk but to all the posts that I had been appointed. I was a broken man, and I went home. And then on the 10th or the 9th of April, my old friend and good acquaintance from my student days found me then, Mr. Praljak. Well, I described all that already. I described our conversation in the statement. I don't know if it's necessary for me to go through it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, thank you, it's not necessary. I would now like to ask you: What was your assessment of General Praljak's behaviour and the manner in which he approached you, precisely because you were such good friends?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was not a friendly conversation. It was a resolute military conversation between a soldier who had already seen action in Croatia, a person who knew what difficult wartime conditions were like, a person who could understand me from the military point of view, and this was a man who spoke to me using clear typical military language, letting me know that this was war and there were no resignations in war, that there were wartime assignments in war, there were commanders and orders that must be obeyed. After that, we worked together well as soldiers. And before that and after that, we were friends, but at that time, at the time of this conversation, it was a purely military conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My last question: Could you explain to the Judges what your intentions and objectives were when you joined the HVO, both the civilian and the military components?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was no other way to fight the enemy. The JNA had occupied 30 per cent -- or, rather, 70 per cent of the country. I have already said -- I don't know how clear I was, because I was interrupted when I wanted to address this topic. The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the session that lasted from the 4th until the 8th of April, 1992, saw at the time when the enemy had already occupied 70 per cent of the country, the Presidency invited the Yugoslav People's Army to intervene in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, they invited it in to occupy the remaining 30 per cent of the territory. And then the Prosecutor after that asked me why we opted for the insignia that we took, why were we not called the BH Army, why did we not place ourselves under the command of the Presidency? What Presidency? The Presidency that invites the JNA to intervene and occupy the remaining 30 per cent of the territory? We had to find some insignia, some emblems that people would be willing to fight under and to fight -- to oppose the JNA, and there was no other possibility for putting together all the municipalities, to organise them, to make it clear to them that they had to fight under the same flag, under the same emblem. We did not have any other option, because I explained to you how municipalities acted. I think this was a very good example.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief, and I would like this statement that bears the number 3D 03216 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exhibit is admitted -- or, rather, we will issue a decision later on that matter. Do other Defence teams have questions to ask? Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems no one has questions to put. Regarding cross-examination by the Prosecution with respect to that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm just going to have one question for the witness. But before that, I just wanted to note for the record that we had previously been provided with the French language version of the 92 ter statement of this witness. It was filed with the Registry. And just for the record, I noted that the first part of paragraph 2 indicates that the witness is referring to mid-April 1999, and so that's clearly a typo, because in the original language and in the English, it refers to 1992. But knowing that the Trial Chamber works on the French, I just thought I would make that clarification. And then my only question for Mr. Buntic on this is to ask whether during this period of time, 1991, whether he knows -- and 1992, whether he knows if General Praljak held a position within the Ministry of Defence for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I don't know what position he held in the Republic of Croatia and until what time. I knew that he did hold some positions in the Republic of Croatia, but I can't give you the exact dates because I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm a little bit confused now, because as far as I know, we provided this statement in B/C/S and in English. I don't know anything about the French translation. In fact, I am caught by surprise by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have in front of me the translation into English of that document. Very well. Witness, your testimony is now over. It's been very long. You stayed for over two weeks, and I was very much afraid that you might stay another week. Luckily, it wasn't so. On behalf of my fellow Judges, I'd like to thank you, and I wish you a safe journey back home. I wish you all the best in your future endeavours as an attorney-at-law. Thank you very much. Could Madam Usher escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be given 15 minutes? That should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. We don't want witnesses to make lengthy statements afterwards. You came here to answer to the questions put to you. We allowed you to make one statement, but no need to go further than that. It is -- you're not entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for calling me here and making it possible for me to talk about the facts that I know of; and I will be happy if my testimony contributes to the establishment of truth and the reaching of a just decision in this case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Mr. Registrar, could we move into private session, because I'd like to deliver a short oral decision in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now in open session. Regarding next week, so that everything is clear, I inform you that we will have Witness Zuzul. He will come here to be cross-examined. He will be heard as of Monday, quarter past 2.00. As far as I remember, the Defence will be allocated two hours and one minute -- well, let's say two hours. Then the Prosecutor will have five hours at his disposal. Unless there are objections, delays or problems of any kind, in principle, we should be able to finish on Tuesday or Wednesday with his testimony. It could be Thursday as well. It all depends. This is what I wanted to inform you about. Are there administrative issues to be raised from the Defence? I see not. From the Prosecution? Not. I wish you all a nice weekend. We shall reconvene on Monday at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of July, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.35 p.m.,
